title: William Henry Harrison

jokes.text: I'm a ninth-level octopriest in the Church of the Reasonableists.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks for evidence to preserve the Newport land; a witness presents religious credentials.
jokes.punchline: The religion is called the 'Reasonableists' and he holds the rank of 'ninth-level octopriest' — bureaucratic specificity applied to obvious nonsense.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of a religion named 'Reasonableists' that is clearly not reasonable, and the mock-bureaucratic precision of 'ninth-level octopriest.' Pawnee's recurring cult is a reliable running gag but still lands here with fresh detail.

dialogue.speaker: Reasonableist
dialogue.line: I have religious evidence for land preservation. My faith teaches that we must protect the natural world because it was created by the Lizard God who lives inside Jupiter's Sphincter.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I... what?

dialogue.speaker: Reasonableist
dialogue.line: The Lizard God demands it. All hail the Sphincter.

jokes.text: The land is sacred in our religion because it's the place where all human souls will be transmuted when Zorp the Lizard God passes through Jupiter's Sphincter.
jokes.setup: The witness explains why the land is religiously significant.
jokes.punchline: The specific eschatology involves a Lizard God and 'Jupiter's Sphincter' — anatomical vulgarity delivered with utter earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'sacred religious land' to 'Jupiter's Sphincter' is a perfect absurdist gut-punch. The deadpan delivery implied by the mockumentary format amplifies it. 'Zorp the Lizard God' is a Pawnee recurring element, but 'Jupiter's Sphincter' is a genuinely creative and committed piece of world-building absurdity that earns a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Reasonableist
dialogue.line: Simple, matter-of-fact cult salute

jokes.text: Hail Zorp.
jokes.setup: The witness has just described the apocalyptic cosmology of their religion.
jokes.punchline: He signs off with 'Hail Zorp' — a deadpan ritual farewell that treats the absurdity as mundane.
jokes.explanation: Two words that do tremendous work. The perfect economy score is justified — it's the entire joke in two syllables. The callback to 'Hail Zorp' as a sign-off mirrors religious salutations and is the ideal button on the absurdist sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to find something—anything—to stop this development. We could be grasping at straws here, but at this point I'm willing to literally grasp at straws if it means saving this land.

jokes.text: So, hold onto your straws, everybody, because Mama's going grasping.
jokes.setup: Leslie admits she's looking for any argument to preserve the land.
jokes.punchline: She self-awarely coins 'Mama's going grasping' as a folksy metaphor for 'grasping at straws,' acknowledging her own desperation with cheerful energy.
jokes.explanation: Extremely Leslie Knope — only she would deliver a pep talk to herself about her own strategic desperation with this level of chipper self-awareness. 'Mama's going grasping' is a quotable Leslieism that earns a high character integration score.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: We need to protect our environment and reduce our carbon footprint. Even small changes add up over time.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Yeah, like the ant population has decreased by 0.003% over the last forty years.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: That's... that's not really the point.

jokes.text: In 1980, there were more than 600 million Indiana Brown Ants in that forest. Today, there are only 595 million. At that rate, they'll all be gone by the year 203060.
jokes.setup: An environmentalist presents data about the declining ant population as evidence of ecological crisis.
jokes.punchline: The math reveals the ants won't all be gone for 200,000 years — undercutting any urgency.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed setup/punchline. The joke builds through specificity — real-sounding numbers delivered with authority — then collapses the urgency entirely. The mathematical absurdity rewards attentive listeners. Solid craft.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Extinction projected 200,000 years in future

jokes.text: Two hundred and three thousand and sixty? Two hundred thousand years from now? Yes. That doesn't seem like an immediate crisis.
jokes.setup: Leslie hears the timeline of ant extinction.
jokes.punchline: Her flat 'That doesn't seem like an immediate crisis' is the straight-man button to the absurdity — but it's also delivered with Leslie's characteristic diplomatic understatement.
jokes.explanation: Functions as the necessary button/callback to joke #5. Leslie's reaction is the payoff, but the joke is mostly set up by the witness. Gets a solid functional score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: We have a crisis on our hands.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The parks department is out of breakfast cereal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: ...Ron, that's not a crisis.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It is to me.

jokes.text: I've got a different idea for that land. An amusement park with rides and food and sexy cartoon characters. I call it Disneyland.
jokes.setup: Leslie's meeting to hear serious arguments for land preservation is interrupted by an unknown figure pitching an idea.
jokes.punchline: The pitch is for Disneyland — already a real thing — delivered as an original idea.
jokes.explanation: Funny non-sequitur. The phrase 'sexy cartoon characters' as a selling point is the best word choice here. The Disneyland reveal is a decent misdirection, though not a deeply original concept.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about an innovative amusement park concept. Picture this: a magical place where families can go and experience wonder and joy together.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ben, that sounds amazing! Have you already—

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I call it Disneyland.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ben, Disney—Walt Disney created Disneyland in 1955.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, I invented it first. In my head. Just now.

jokes.text: How did you get in here? Broke a window.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how the interloper gained entry to the meeting.
jokes.punchline: The utterly matter-of-fact 'Broke a window' — treating vandalism as the most natural explanation.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact. The deadpan economy is exceptional. The joke is in the total absence of shame or explanation. Not the most original premise but executed with perfect minimalism.

dialogue.line: Matter-of-fact admission of breaking and entering

jokes.text: You guys, I am Roscoe. I am Vice President of Cool New Shizz here at Gryzzl.
jokes.setup: A Gryzzl executive introduces himself and his title.
jokes.punchline: 'Vice President of Cool New Shizz' is a satirical Silicon Valley job title — corporate authority wrapped in faux-casual language.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satire of tech-bro culture. The title is funny on its own, but also establishes Gryzzl's entire comedic register. 'Shizz' as a sanitized corporate euphemism is well-observed.

dialogue.speaker: Roscoe
dialogue.line: I'd like to introduce our new Vice President of Stratgic Initiatives.

jokes.text: Feel free in this meeting to break out your vapes and just kick back.
jokes.setup: Roscoe opens a business meeting.
jokes.punchline: He invites attendees to vape during a professional meeting, as if this is standard hospitality.
jokes.explanation: Functional satire of tech office culture. Part of the Roscoe/Gryzzl comedic package — works as texture but isn't a standout joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Alright team, let's have a brainstorm session about this new initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Tech Bro
dialogue.line: Actually, I prefer to call it a brain tornado. It's more disruptive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A brain tornado?

dialogue.speaker: Tech Bro
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's like a brainstorm, but it destroys everything in its path and nobody knows why it happened.

jokes.text: So, we had this far-out brain tornado. / Good idea.
jokes.setup: Roscoe uses tech-bro slang ('brain tornado') for 'brainstorm.'
jokes.punchline: Ben flatly translates: 'Good idea.' — cutting through the jargon with exhausted efficiency.
jokes.explanation: Ben's two-word deflation of Roscoe's language is a great deadpan. The economy of the straight-man response is almost perfect. Works as a duo joke — Roscoe sets up the absurdity, Ben punctures it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: We need to leverage some celebrity endorsements to really synergize our brand activation and create maximum engagement metrics.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Yes! We should get someone super relatable and on-brand. Someone who really understands the core values of what we're trying to do.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo. That's what I'm talking about. We gotta get a celebrity that's got that street cred, you know what I'm saying? Someone who can really connect with the youth demographic and create that viral moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Maybe we could approach someone like...

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Jerry, nobody cares what you think.

jokes.text: We should get a brity to come kick it with us small-time and then just be like, 'Hey, chums. Let's get tight with Gryzz.'
jokes.setup: Roscoe pitches the idea of getting a celebrity endorsement.
jokes.punchline: The actual proposed script — 'Hey, chums. Let's get tight with Gryzz' — is so clueless about how celebrity endorsements work that it's absurdist.
jokes.explanation: Part of the Roscoe language-satire throughline. 'Chums' and 'get tight with Gryzz' as imagined celebrity dialogue is moderately funny tech-bro parody.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't need flash. I prefer quality. Like, I would rather have one nice thing than ten cheap things.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: For example, I would rather have one shoe than ten shoes.

jokes.text: That's why I refuse to write my signature in cursive.
jokes.setup: Someone argues for quality over flash in business.
jokes.punchline: Ron's illustration of 'quality over flash' is his refusal to write in cursive — a personal quirk elevated to philosophical principle.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Ron Swanson character comedy. The jump from 'quality over flash' to 'cursive signatures' is perfectly Ron — treating a minor aesthetic preference as a deeply principled stance. The economy is nearly perfect. Could only be Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Elton John has a whole chain of restaurants with Chick-fil-A. It's called Elton's.

jokes.text: The Nets wouldn't be in Brooklyn if it weren't for Jay Z. And the sales for Chick-fil-A went through the roof once Elton John bought them.
jokes.setup: Tom argues celebrities can help a business cause, citing real examples.
jokes.punchline: The Jay Z/Nets example is real; the Elton John/Chick-fil-A claim is completely fabricated — and Chick-fil-A's anti-LGBTQ+ stance makes Elton John the most absurdly wrong celebrity to own it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is masterful: anchor the audience with a real fact (Jay Z/Nets), then immediately follow with a fabricated one that is specifically absurd because of the political incongruity (Elton John owning the famously anti-gay Chick-fil-A). Tom delivers it with equal confidence, making it a perfect deadpan misdirection. Highly quotable, earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: We need to synergize our paradigms and frack your brainiums to leverage some disruptive innovation in the space.

jokes.text: The only celebrities I recognize are furniture maker Garry Knox Bennett, designer of the notorious 16-penny nail cabinet, and Magnus, the 5x5 bull elk I saw near my cabin two years ago.
jokes.setup: Ron is asked to think of celebrity suggestions and protests he has no interest in celebrities.
jokes.punchline: His list of 'celebrities' is: an obscure furniture maker and an elk he once saw. Delivered in a talking-head confessional with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's finest jokes. Only Ron Swanson would recognize a furniture craftsman and a specific named elk as the two celebrities worthy of his attention. 'Magnus, the 5x5 bull elk' is a masterpiece of character-specific absurdism — the naming of the elk, the exact rack measurement, the personal sighting. Perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, I understood none of that, but I'm going to nod and back away slowly.

jokes.text: Took a shot at the bastard, and he stuck his antlers through the door of my meat shed.
jokes.setup: Ron is describing Magnus the elk.
jokes.punchline: The feud between Ron and an elk is escalated — Ron shot at him and the elk retaliated by destroying his meat shed.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the Ron/elk feud — complete with a 'meat shed' — is wonderfully specific. The fact that Ron owns a 'meat shed' is itself a joke. Ron referring to an elk as 'the bastard' with personal grievance is character comedy at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't care about celebrities. My heroes are a obscure furniture maker from the 1800s and a wild elk I saw once.

jokes.text: One day, Magnus, I will wear you as a jacket.
jokes.setup: Ron is recounting his ongoing feud with Magnus the elk.
jokes.punchline: His vow of vengeance — to literally wear the elk as a jacket — is delivered with the weight of a sacred oath.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. 'One day, Magnus, I will wear you as a jacket' is a perfect line. It escalates the feud to an absurd promise of revenge-as-fashion, is utterly specific to Ron's character (hunter, craftsman, grudge-holder), has perfect economy, and is among the most quotable lines in the episode. The direct address to the elk — 'Magnus' — as though he might one day read the transcript seals it. This approaches the 9.5 anchor level in character integration and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That elk, Magnus, has made this personal. When I find him, I'm going to wear his hide as a coat. I'm going to wear his antlers as a hat. I'm going to feed his hooves to the other elk, just to send a message.

jokes.text: Have you thought about this? You could be an airline pilot. / I don't like heights. / What about a submarine pilot? / I don't like depths.
jokes.setup: April and Andy are playing a game to find Andy a career. April suggests airline pilot.
jokes.punchline: Andy doesn't like heights; submarine pilot is suggested; Andy doesn't like depths — a perfectly symmetrical absurdist refusal.
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-structured joke. The parallel construction (heights/airline, depths/submarine) is satisfying, and Andy's reflexive disqualification of every option fits his character. Solid sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You could be a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A lawyer?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: An engineer?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What do you want to do?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Nothing. I want to do nothing and die.

jokes.text: I don't like anything, okay? You're not gonna be able to find a career for me. So, just give up.
jokes.setup: April keeps trying to find Andy a career.
jokes.punchline: Andy's flat declaration 'I don't like anything' as a career-ending conclusion, delivered not with sadness but casual certainty.
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy — Andy's blithe self-defeatism is very him. But it's a familiar beat in the Andy/career subplot and doesn't offer much new ground.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're playing a word game to find career ideas. I'll give you a category, and you say the first word that comes to mind.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, first category: things that are bouncy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Trampoline.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Good! Next: things that are soft.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Trampoline.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, things that fly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Trampoline.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, trampolines don't fly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Executive. / Trampoline. / Computer. / Trampoline.
jokes.setup: April proposes a word-association game to find Andy a career.
jokes.punchline: Andy's responses are 'Trampoline' twice — the second time even more committed, suggesting he actively wants to work with trampolines but only trampolines.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. The repetition of 'Trampoline' is funnier the second time, and the implied rhythm of the word-association game makes the structure sing. Andy's one-track mind is perfectly expressed in two words. One of the best-structured micro-jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you need me to sign some documents?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, but first... *leans in seductively* ...you have to sleep with me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just kidding, I'm not gonna do that. Sign here.

jokes.text: There's no way that I will be in the same room with Ron Swanson unless it is during a police lineup when I am pointing him out as the man who betrayed me.
jokes.setup: Ben asks Leslie to go sign documents in the same room as Ron.
jokes.punchline: Leslie rejects it — but invents an elaborate scenario where she would accept: a police lineup where she identifies Ron as a criminal.
jokes.explanation: Strong Leslie character comedy. The specificity of 'during a police lineup when I am pointing him out as the man who betrayed me' takes it from a simple refusal to an entire dramatic fantasy. Very Leslie to have already scripted this scene in her head.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I could pick Ron out of a lineup from a mile away. I'd know that stoic face, those piercing eyes, that magnificent mustache anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They could put him in a fake beard, a wig, different clothes, and I'd still spot him immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? They could dye his mustache blonde, give him a facelift, teach him to smile, and I would STILL recognize Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I will never not see Ron in a lineup. That is a fact.

jokes.text: 'That's him, officer! Ronald Swanson.' 'Thank you, Leslie, that's the fifth crime you've solved this month. I'm not supposed to do this, but let me give you a badge and...'
jokes.setup: Leslie is narrating her fantasy police lineup scenario.
jokes.punchline: The fantasy escalates: she's apparently solved five crimes this month and is about to receive a badge — Leslie has invented an entire hero arc for herself.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the fantasy — from pointing out Ron to receiving a badge for solving five crimes — is a perfect encapsulation of Leslie's grandiosity and self-mythology. 'That's the fifth crime you've solved this month' is an inspired detail. Could only be Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chief, I'd like to request a badge. I'm ready to become an honorary detective.

dialogue.speaker: Chief
dialogue.line: Knope, you're not qualified.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not qualified? I've solved crimes in this town that the actual police couldn't solve. Remember when I found out who was stealing from the Parks Department? Me. I also figured out who was leaving anonymous complaints about the swing set. Also me.

dialogue.speaker: Chief
dialogue.line: That's not how any of this works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine. I'll just take my detective skills elsewhere. Pawnee Police Department's loss. Eagleton's gain.

jokes.text: Could you please focus? / 'I'm not supposed to do this, but let me give you a badge and...'
jokes.setup: Ben interrupts Leslie's police-lineup fantasy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie resumes the fantasy mid-interruption, unwilling to leave the scene before she gets her badge.
jokes.explanation: The callback where Leslie refuses to end her fantasy even after being interrupted adds a layer — the joke escalates because she can't let go of the badge. Solid structure.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I was just gonna tell you guys a personal story, but now that I'm thinking about it, this is really depressing.

jokes.text: I recently had a bit of a health scare, just a couple weeks in the hospital. Oh, God. This story's terrible so far.
jokes.setup: A character overhears the notary problem and starts sharing a personal anecdote beginning with a hospitalization.
jokes.punchline: Ben's interruption — 'Oh, God. This story's terrible so far' — is the perfect deadpan audience surrogate reaction to an oversharing stranger.
jokes.explanation: Ben's 'Oh, God. This story's terrible so far' is a genuinely funny interruption — self-aware, character-appropriate, and lands on the exact right beat. The setup (hospitalization) creates dread that Ben voices for the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: You know what? Life's too short. I'm going to pursue my dreams. I'm going to become a notary public.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I've already got the stamp picked out.

jokes.text: So, I fulfilled one of my lifelong dreams, and I became a Notary Public.
jokes.setup: Character was motivated by a near-death hospital experience to live life to the fullest.
jokes.punchline: His 'lifelong dream' is becoming a notary public — a deliberately anticlimactic aspiration after a health scare.
jokes.explanation: Near-death epiphany → becomes a notary is a perfectly calibrated anticlimactic joke. The structure is clean and the misdirection works well. The specificity of notary public (not even a glamorous legal role) is the key.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: How long is this feud going to last?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Until you apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not going to apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then it lasts forever. Those are the rules.

jokes.text: And then you can tell Ron to rot in hell.
jokes.setup: Leslie agrees to Ben's plan for signing documents separately.
jokes.punchline: She tacks on 'and then you can tell Ron to rot in hell' as though it's a logistical step in the plan, delivered casually.
jokes.explanation: Functional character joke. Leslie treating 'rot in hell' as a practical instruction is a good Leslie-ism but doesn't rise to the level of her best jokes in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not that famous. I mean, sure, I've been on some lists, but...

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, you wrote your own name on the list.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, yeah, but that's different.

jokes.text: No, I'm not. And infinity plus one year.
jokes.setup: Ben accuses Leslie of acting like a little kid about the feud.
jokes.punchline: Leslie denies it — then immediately proves it by responding with 'infinity plus one year,' a playground argument tactic.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The structure is perfect: deny being childish, then immediately use the most childish possible comeback. 'Infinity plus one year' is an inspired escalation that belongs in the child's toolbox and nowhere else. The self-contradiction in a single breath is beautifully constructed and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Bloosh magazine? That's the worst thing I've ever heard of. It's a lifestyle magazine for people who have given up on life. All pictures of throw pillows and recipes that use 'unexpected ingredients.' I would rather read a phone book. Actually, I would rather read a phone book out loud at a city council meeting.

jokes.text: That's nice, but I don't know if you can really consider me a celebrity. / Yeah. That's your handwriting.
jokes.setup: Tom Haverford is suggested as a celebrity candidate; he demurs modestly.
jokes.punchline: Ben points out that Tom submitted his own name — undermining the modesty entirely.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured two-beat joke. Tom's false modesty is immediately exposed by his own handwriting on the list. Great character comedy — Tom is exactly the kind of person who submits himself and then acts humble about it. The reveal is clean and well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Bloosh is a legitimate news source. He won a Pulitzer Prize for listicles.

jokes.text: Bloosh has won the Pulitzer Prize for best top ten listicle two years in a row.
jokes.setup: Someone defends Annabel Porter's Bloosh as a serious publication.
jokes.punchline: The Pulitzer Prize has apparently added a 'best top ten listicle' category — a satire of the degradation of prestige media.
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire. 'Pulitzer Prize for best top ten listicle' nails the absurdity of clickbait being elevated to prize-worthy journalism. Concise and pointed.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: I wrote a book about President William Henry Harrison.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: What's it called?

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: "William Henry Harrison: A Very Long Time Ago."

jokes.text: We're also a little ashamed of him because he didn't wear a coat at his inauguration, caught a bad cold and died 32 days later. He's an embarrassing footnote. But he's our embarrassing footnote.
jokes.setup: Bill is explaining Pawnee's complicated relationship with William Henry Harrison.
jokes.punchline: 'He's an embarrassing footnote. But he's our embarrassing footnote.' — civic pride attached to a genuinely ridiculous historical figure.
jokes.explanation: 'He's an embarrassing footnote. But he's our embarrassing footnote.' is an excellent line. It perfectly parodies local civic pride, and the historical truth (Harrison died of pneumonia after refusing to wear a coat) makes the joke both accurate and absurd. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Dude, spoilers! I haven't gotten to that part of history yet.

jokes.text: Barely a President. William Henry Harrison's Thirty-Two Days in the White House.
jokes.setup: Bill announces the title of his self-published biography.
jokes.punchline: The title 'Barely a President' is a perfect deadpan assessment of Harrison's presidency — honest to the point of self-defeating advocacy.
jokes.explanation: 'Barely a President' is a wonderfully frank title for a historical biography — it's the kind of honest self-sabotage that characterizes Pawnee local experts. Great economy, and the subtitle doubles down with precision.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This biography of William Henry Harrison is putting me to sleep. He was president for like a month.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, don't disrespect President Harrison like that. He was a great man.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He died of pneumonia. That's not greatness, that's poor immune system.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not going to sit here and listen to you trash talk one of America's heroes.

jokes.text: Um, spoilers much? Now I'll never read that book.
jokes.setup: Bill reveals Harrison had an unknown hunting lodge on the Newport land — the major finding from his biography.
jokes.punchline: Andy complains about spoilers for a presidential biography — as if the historical details were the twists he was looking forward to.
jokes.explanation: Very Andy. Applying the spoiler-aversion logic of pop culture to a 19th century presidential biography is precisely the kind of confused earnestness that defines the character. Great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a product idea I'd like you to consider investing in.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's called Rent-a-Swag. You rent cool stuff to people who aren't cool.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The slogan is: 'Swag for the Tragically Uncool.'

jokes.text: Which would be icing on the cake, not the reason why we're doing this.
jokes.setup: Leslie expresses excitement about using the Harrison lodge to 'stick it to Ron's team.'
jokes.punchline: She immediately catches herself and adds the diplomatic disclaimer — but the damage is done; clearly revenge is at least part of the motivation.
jokes.explanation: Functional character joke. Leslie's self-correction is a recurring pattern in the show — it works but isn't surprising. Gets a solid but unremarkable score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Terry, what is Leslie planning?

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: Oh, Leslie's organizing a surprise birthday party for you next Friday at the community center. She's already ordered the cake and everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Thank you, Terry.

jokes.text: That book sounded so boring, I cried a little. Oh, babe, I'm sorry you had to hear that. You're safe now.
jokes.setup: Bill has been describing the Harrison biography.
jokes.punchline: April reports crying from boredom; Andy treats it as a trauma with 'You're safe now.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'You're safe now' — treating April's boredom as a genuine danger survived — is a sweet absurdist beat. The couple's dynamic is nicely expressed in two lines.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, look at all these bricks. I want to buy these bricks.

jokes.text: Terry, what's Leslie up to? / She is trying to find a historical reason to earmark the land for preservation. / Terry, come on, man.
jokes.setup: Ben has just told Ron he won't share Leslie's plans. Ron immediately turns to Terry.
jokes.punchline: Terry instantly betrays the confidence; Ron is exasperated at how easy it was. The running gag of Terry being treated as irrelevant but also as a reliable information source.
jokes.explanation: The Terry gag works on Parks and Rec because of how immediately it undercuts Ben's diplomatic posturing. Ron's 'Terry, come on, man' is the perfect note of exasperation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is a bag of old hamburgers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How old?

jokes.text: Now, will you please consider investing in that toddler cologne I've been bugging you about? / Toddler cologne. / Baby, you smell good.
jokes.setup: Tom tries to leverage Ron's moment of openness to pitch a business idea.
jokes.punchline: The business idea is 'toddler cologne' — he even provides the tagline: 'Baby, you smell good.'
jokes.explanation: Tom's business ideas are a reliable joke engine, but 'toddler cologne' with the tagline 'Baby, you smell good' is genuinely inspired. The tagline functions as both a product slogan and an implicit endorsement from a baby. Very quotable, Tom-specific absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, Andy, that's just a old soda can.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Are you kidding? This could be from the 1980s. That's practically ancient.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's from this morning. I threw it away.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Even better. Fresh artifacts.

jokes.text: Here we are, like, 'Here's the place where I buried the map that will show us the way to William Henry Harrison's awesome hunting cabin?'
jokes.setup: The group arrives at the location of Harrison's hunting lodge.
jokes.punchline: Andy interprets the journey as an adventure movie where someone buried a treasure map to reach this point.
jokes.explanation: Andy being Andy — but a bit rambling. The joke is in the concept (treating a historical site visit like a treasure hunt) but the execution is wordy and doesn't land as sharply as his best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Maybe we just don't mention the missing page.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: No. We have to tell them. It's the right thing to do.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'm a notary public. I took an oath. Well, technically I took an oath to uphold the oath that I took when I became a notary public.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: And I took an oath to uphold that oath as well.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: So that's like three oaths. Maybe four.

jokes.text: Babe, we should sell our dumb house and buy this one.
jokes.setup: The group arrives at the Harrison 'hunting lodge,' which is clearly a collapsed ruin.
jokes.punchline: Andy sincerely wants to move into the crumbling ruins — his standards are cheerfully non-existent.
jokes.explanation: Solid Andy joke. 'Our dumb house' compared favorably to a pile of ruins is funny and character-appropriate. Works better with visual context of the actual ruins.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, look at this entire room dedicated to what would have happened if William Henry Harrison had worn a coat that day.

jokes.text: I mean, literally. There's a bag of old hamburgers over there. / What? How old?
jokes.setup: Ben says the hunting lodge is literally garbage.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate concern is the age of the hamburgers — not the historical significance, not that they're garbage, but how old specifically.
jokes.explanation: 'How old?' is a great Andy Dwyer reaction — his implicit interest in whether the hamburgers are potentially edible is perfectly in character. Economy is strong and character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And this room is dedicated to people who had their fifteen minutes of fame and then completely disappeared. We're calling it the Harrison William Henry room, because he was president for like a month and then died.

jokes.text: And a different notary notarized the oath I signed.
jokes.setup: The notary explains the seriousness of his oath.
jokes.punchline: There was a second notary involved specifically to notarize the notarization — an infinite regress of bureaucratic solemnity.
jokes.explanation: The meta-notarization is a great absurdist escalation of the notary subplot. The implied infinite regression of notaries is the comedic image that makes this work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We paid $15 to get in and all they had was a broken dinosaur and a painting of a guy that looked like he was dying. For $15, I could've bought a pizza and watched a guy actually die on TV.

jokes.text: William Henry Harrison is totally ridiculous. They can't even fill a small museum with real stuff about his life because he was so lame.
jokes.setup: The group is at the Harrison museum, surveying the available historical material.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, his supposed champion, admits in a talking-head that he was 'so lame' they can't fill even a small museum.
jokes.explanation: Works as Leslie self-undermining her own argument. The bluntness of 'he was so lame' from an ordinarily enthusiastic booster is the comedic note.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And they're charging fifteen dollars admission? Fifteen dollars! That's an insult. I could go to a real museum for that price. I could go to... well, I could go somewhere better.

jokes.text: The 'If He'd Worn A Coat' room explores how great America would have been if Harrison had worn a coat at his inauguration and not died.
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing the museum rooms.
jokes.punchline: An entire room dedicated to the counterfactual history of a coat.
jokes.explanation: This is great absurdist local-museum comedy. The 'If He'd Worn A Coat' room is a perfectly silly concept that also satirizes the earnestness of small-town historical societies. The room name is the entire joke and it's very well-named.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We should get a giant hamster ball and roll around in it!

jokes.text: This room is called Other Things That Were Famous For One Month.
jokes.setup: The Harrison museum has multiple themed rooms.
jokes.punchline: Harrison is implicitly grouped with 'Other Things That Were Famous For One Month' — the museum's own exhibit contextualizes him as ephemeral.
jokes.explanation: A museum room called 'Other Things That Were Famous For One Month' is a quietly devastating joke about Harrison's legacy. The economy of the room name doing all the work is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is... nice. Very nice. I appreciate the natural light. And these throw pillows. Excellent throw pillows. Is that a scented candle? Wonderful. Lavender, I presume? Delightful. I could really see myself... absolutely hating every second I spend in here.

jokes.text: Oh, and side note, admission to this museum costs $14.
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing the Harrison museum's meager contents.
jokes.punchline: After establishing the museum barely has content, she notes admission is $14 — an overcharge for what amounts to almost nothing.
jokes.explanation: A good punctuation joke after the museum section. The $14 charge for a museum with almost nothing is a recognizable real-world absurdity delivered dryly.

jokes.text: During the election campaign of 1840, William Henry Harrison supporters rolled this 10-foot tin and paper ball down country lanes all across America... Why? Was there something inside the stupid ball? / Ooh! Like a giant hamster?
jokes.setup: Leslie enthusiastically explains the famous Tippecanoe tin ball campaign prop.
jokes.punchline: Ben and Andy respond not with historical interest but with confusion about the ball's utility — Andy's 'Like a giant hamster?' is the perfect absurdist escalation.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Leslie's genuine historical enthusiasm with Ben's pragmatic skepticism and Andy's hamster theory is excellent. 'Like a giant hamster?' is a perfectly absurd Andy contribution.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you just said, and I'm not gonna pretend like I do.

jokes.text: We are up against a very flashy Internet company, and we should be aiming for quantity over quality.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to spin the situation — they have almost no real Harrison material.
jokes.punchline: Her solution is explicitly 'quantity over quality' — an inversion of every argument she would normally make.
jokes.explanation: Works as a character joke — Leslie abandoning her standards is inherently funny. But it's a setup for more jokes rather than a strong joke in itself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: You want to know what's trending right now? Artisanal ice cubes made from melted snow that fell on a billionaire's estate. Gold-plated phone chargers shaped like tiny gavels. And my personal favorite: luxury air that's been breathed by celebrities and then bottled.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Exactly. That's why it's trending.

jokes.text: Wow! This is exactly what I imagined heaven looks like. Right down to the unisex linen tunics.
jokes.setup: Ron enters Annabel Porter's lifestyle boutique/space — the antithesis of everything he values.
jokes.punchline: His deadpan description of it as his vision of heaven — complete with 'unisex linen tunics' — is Ron expressing maximum contempt through faux-enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: One of Ron's best jokes in the episode. 'Unisex linen tunics' as the specific detail he uses to condemn this lifestyle space is inspired — it's the detail that most offends his masculine, utilitarian sensibility. The deadpan of 'exactly what I imagined heaven looks like' is perfect Swanson irony.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Beef milk is literally just regular milk described pretentiously

jokes.text: I'm sorry I'm late for our coven. I was polishing my oyster forks with a cage-free olive oil rub.
jokes.setup: Annabel Porter arrives at the meeting with Tom and Ron.
jokes.punchline: She apologizes for being late because she was polishing oyster forks — and the olive oil used was specifically 'cage-free,' which is a label for eggs not oil.
jokes.explanation: Excellent lifestyle-satire comedy. 'Cage-free olive oil rub' is inspired because cage-free is an animal welfare label applied to an oil that has no cage concerns — it's the ultimate virtue-signaling word salad. 'Polishing my oyster forks' is itself absurd as a reason for lateness.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Beef milk is just milk.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: No, it's different. It's artisanal. I'm charging $12 a carton.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: For milk?

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: For *artisanal* milk. People will pay anything if you say it's artisanal.

jokes.text: Apology accepted, and then I have no reaction to anything else you said.
jokes.setup: Annabel makes an elaborate, jargon-filled apology.
jokes.punchline: Tom accepts the apology, then explicitly declares he has no reaction to the rest — a masterfully polite dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Tom's 'I have no reaction to anything else you said' is a great line — more cutting than confusion or outrage, because the no-reaction is the poliest possible dismissal. High economy, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: People are actually waiting to pay for overpriced milk

jokes.text: This season, I'm intrigued by asymmetrical overalls, angora toothbrushes, and locally sourced Italian flip-flops.
jokes.setup: Ron asks what's in right now in lifestyle trends.
jokes.punchline: Annabel's trend list includes 'angora toothbrushes' — a product that doesn't exist and whose existence would be pointless — alongside other pretentious micro-trend items.
jokes.explanation: 'Angora toothbrushes' is the standout in this list — it's exactly the kind of absurd luxury item that would appear in a real lifestyle newsletter, and its impracticality (soft angora fiber = terrible toothbrush) is the joke. 'Locally sourced Italian flip-flops' is a near-oxymoron that also lands well.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I love how you're not intimidating, you're not condescending, and you have no idea what you're talking about. It's refreshing.

jokes.text: Now, try the hottest new craze, beef milk. It's like almond milk that's been squeezed through tiny holes in living cows. / That's milk. / No. Milk costs $3 a gallon. Annabel's authentic, hand-strained teat-to-table Beef Milk? That costs $60 a gallon. Yeah. And there's a wait list.
jokes.setup: Annabel introduces 'beef milk' as a new beverage trend.
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat 'That's milk' is the perfect straight-man response, but the escalation comes from Tom immediately seeing the business genius — including the term 'teat-to-table,' the $60/gallon price, and the waitlist.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best extended joke. The layered structure is exceptional: (1) 'beef milk' as a fake trend, (2) the definition ('squeezed through tiny holes in living cows') which is technically accurate for milk but reframed as artisan, (3) Ron's perfect one-word response ('That's milk'), (4) the rebrand to 'teat-to-table Beef Milk' at $60/gallon, (5) Tom's endorsement and the waitlist. Each layer escalates the absurdity while each character reacts perfectly in type. 'Teat-to-table' is one of the best coinages in the episode. Approaches the 9.5 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Bill Burgers
dialogue.line: It's an unpaid volunteer position at the museum.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, you get to work in a museum! That's worth something.

dialogue.speaker: Bill Burgers
dialogue.line: The only payment is museum bucks — worthless currency you can only use at the single vending machine in the break room.

jokes.text: It's like almond milk that's been squeezed through tiny holes in living cows.
jokes.setup: 'Beef milk' has been introduced as a trend.
jokes.punchline: Annabel describes it as almond milk 'squeezed through tiny holes in living cows' — which is just a spectacularly convoluted description of regular milk.
jokes.explanation: The episode's second-best joke behind 'I will wear you as a jacket.' The punchline is structurally perfect: she defines beef milk in a way that makes it sound exotic and artisanal, and then you realize she has just described milk. 'Squeezed through tiny holes in living cows' is a beautiful piece of writing — every word does work. The callback/button (Ron's 'That's milk') makes it even better as a two-parter. Exceptional originality and structure.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have three main interests: government, breakfast foods, and the structural integrity of bridges.

jokes.text: Terry, what is Leslie up to? / Getting ready for a big press conference. / Terry, come on!
jokes.setup: Ben again refuses to share plans; Ron again immediately asks Terry.
jokes.punchline: Terry again immediately answers; Ben's exasperation escalates.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Terry-as-information-leak gag is functional and gets a reasonable laugh, but it's a repeat of the same structure without meaningful escalation. Loses some points for originality as a direct callback.

jokes.text: I just wanted to say that I really like your museum. It's weird and sad and unnecessary.
jokes.setup: Andy approaches the museum curator after visiting.
jokes.punchline: His compliment is the honest description: 'weird and sad and unnecessary' — delivered as sincere praise.
jokes.explanation: Andy's compliment/insult is a perfect character moment. 'Weird and sad and unnecessary' as genuine praise is Andy at his best — he means it kindly, and somehow it is a compliment from him. Excellent economy and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Did you know that notaries have been around since ancient Rome? We're basically the backbone of civilization.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wow, that's... that's incredible, Craig. I had no idea notaries were so important.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Right? And get this — we can notarize up to 500 documents per day if we really hustle.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: 500 documents. In one day. That is absolutely fascinating.

jokes.text: Sorry, everyone here is a volunteer. Though you do get a yearly stipend of 50,000 Harrison Bucks. Accepted only at that vending machine.
jokes.setup: Andy asks about a museum curator position.
jokes.punchline: The museum pays in its own currency — 'Harrison Bucks' — which is accepted only at a single vending machine on site.
jokes.explanation: Harrison Bucks accepted only at a single vending machine is wonderful small-museum absurdism. The specificity of 'that vending machine' — implying he's pointing at one in the corner — makes it land with a visual quality even in a transcript. A great sight-gag/absurdist joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so April likes... um... let's see. She likes being sarcastic. She likes... not smiling. She likes... making me feel bad about myself.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: She likes having no regard for human life or safety. She likes chaos. She likes... planning things with no regard for how they'll actually turn out.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm just describing myself now.

jokes.text: The only things I like are dogs, sleeping late, and weird birthmarks. You can't make museums about those.
jokes.setup: Andy tries to suggest a career idea involving April starting her own museum.
jokes.punchline: April's list of interests — 'dogs, sleeping late, and weird birthmarks' — is characteristically macabre and contrarian, ending with the deflating 'you can't make museums about those.'
jokes.explanation: The specific inclusion of 'weird birthmarks' in April's interest list is perfectly April — slightly creepy, inexplicably specific, and undercuts the warmth of dogs/sleeping. The deflating 'you can't make museums about those' is the right button. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So April likes... people and dogs. You know what they have in common? They both have four legs... wait, no. People have two legs. Dogs have four legs. So nothing. April just likes things with legs.

jokes.text: I'm not signing anything he's signing. / Did you just hear what I said? / No, of course you didn't. Because I'm a ghost.
jokes.setup: The notary expresses existential despair about being ignored.
jokes.punchline: He concludes he must be a ghost — having died and entered purgatory — because Leslie and Ron are completely ignoring his notary crisis.
jokes.explanation: The notary's 'I'm a ghost' spiral is a good absurdist extension of the running notary gag. The internal logic — he's so ignored he must be dead — is well-constructed and specific to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: If you trace your family tree back far enough, you might be related to George Washington.

dialogue.speaker: Zach
dialogue.line: Wait, really? I might be related to George Washington?

jokes.text: I'm definitely going to wake up tomorrow morning with the same forms for you to sign. Because I've died somehow and now I'm a ghost living in purgatory until I complete my unfinished business.
jokes.setup: The notary expresses frustration about the endless document saga.
jokes.punchline: The full ghost-in-purgatory theory: he's dead, stuck in bureaucratic purgatory, and the 'unfinished business' is notarizing this one document.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the ghost metaphor is well-done — the 'unfinished business' framing is a nice specific touch. Works as part of the notary character's comic arc.

dialogue.speaker: Zach
dialogue.line: Thank you all for coming. I'm here to announce my candidacy with dignity and grace.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Mr. Zach, isn't it true you once got your head stuck in a canoe at Camp Kickapoo?

dialogue.speaker: Zach
dialogue.line: That was one time and it was very humid that day.

jokes.text: One. A distant nephew named Zach Harrison.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Harrison has any living descendants.
jokes.punchline: There is exactly one — a 'distant nephew' — the smallest possible connection to American presidential lineage.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup joke for the Zach Harrison payoff. The joke is in the 'one' and 'distant nephew' — a barely-there lineage — which primes the audience for how underwhelming Zach will be.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This building is incredibly historically significant. George Washington slept here, Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in this very room, and—you know what, I'm just making this up as I go.

jokes.text: This is our guy! American royalty! His veins pulse with the blood of our storied forefathers!
jokes.setup: Leslie hears there is one distant nephew of Harrison.
jokes.punchline: She immediately elevates him to 'American royalty' with veins that 'pulse with the blood of our storied forefathers' — the rhetoric is wildly disproportionate to 'distant nephew.'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's rhetoric-to-reality gap is a reliable comedy engine, and this is a solid execution. 'His veins pulse with the blood of our storied forefathers' applied to someone we'll soon learn is a camp-boner story is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're a direct descendant of William Henry Harrison?

dialogue.speaker: Zach
dialogue.line: Yeah, but it's not that big a deal. He was only president for like a month before he died.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A month? That's still the presidency!

dialogue.speaker: Zach
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm like the great-great-great-grandson. There's a lot of greats between me and any actual accomplishment.

jokes.text: I went to camp with this guy. No one would ride in the boat with him because he had terrible BO. Then, he went with Janine, our counselor, and he fell asleep and got a boner.
jokes.setup: Leslie builds up Zach Harrison as 'American royalty.'
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately deflates the mythology with a detailed camp memory involving Zach's body odor and an involuntary erection in front of a counselor.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Leslie's 'American royalty' rhetoric via Andy's camp story is perfectly structured. The specificity (BO, Janine the counselor, falling asleep) is what makes it funny rather than crude. Andy casually relating this to Leslie's patriotic speech is great character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: And so the ball rolled slowly down the street, much like Leslie's campaign hopes.

jokes.text: I made a list of everything that I know you like. Playing with our dog, staring contests, sex with me, etc. And then, I lost the list. So, I had to make a new list. I didn't have any paper, so I wrote it on my leg. And that's when my leg fell asleep.
jokes.setup: Andy tells April he's been working on figuring out her interests.
jokes.punchline: The story escalates: he lost the list, rewrote it on his leg, and his leg fell asleep — each step more helplessly Andy than the last.
jokes.explanation: Andy at his most Andy. The escalation of failures — lost the list, no paper, wrote on leg, leg fell asleep — is perfectly constructed slapstick-adjacent escalation. 'And that's when my leg fell asleep' as a sentence is inherently funny. 'Sex with me, etc.' being on the list of April's interests is also a great detail.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They call themselves 'Somebody's Daughter dancers.' I assume the name refers to the fact that they are, in fact, somebody's daughter.

jokes.text: Zach! Camp Wamapoke. You got a boner. / We'll catch up. / What a dick.
jokes.setup: Zach Harrison arrives at the press conference. Andy recognizes him from camp.
jokes.punchline: Andy's greeting reduces their entire shared history to 'You got a boner' — perfectly casual. Leslie's exasperated 'What a dick' after Zach walks away is the button.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Zach camp story is excellent. Andy reducing their reunion to 'You got a boner' is incredibly funny in its casualness, and Leslie's reaction ('What a dick') is a perfect double meaning — she's calling Andy out for the greeting while also commenting on Zach. High economy and strong callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: We're leveraging synergistic paradigms with blockchain-adjacent methodologies to maximize our core competencies and disruptive innovation vectors.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: Our dashboard-centric approach integrates machine learning optimization with artisanal hand-crafted experiences, all while maintaining our commitment to holistic wellness and bespoke concierge services.

jokes.text: Ron, what are you doing here? / Setting up for our press conference, which will take place immediately after yours.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives for her press conference and finds Ron already there.
jokes.punchline: Ron has scheduled his competing press conference immediately after hers — a ruthlessly efficient ambush with no pretense of subtlety.
jokes.explanation: Very Ron — the audacity and directness of scheduling his press conference as an immediate follow-up to Leslie's is a perfect expression of his competitive nature. No explanation, no apology.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why are we still signing things? We've signed everything. We've signed documents about signing documents.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is purgatory. We're stuck in bureaucratic purgatory, and the only way out is to sign our way through an infinite loop of forms that generate more forms.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Dante had nine circles of Hell. Parks and Recreation has nine filing cabinets.

jokes.text: Do you want me to bite him? / No.
jokes.setup: Ron appears at Leslie's press conference location; tension rises.
jokes.punchline: April offers to bite Ron — a completely sincere offer that Leslie declines as a logistical consideration rather than a moral one.
jokes.explanation: Two lines, maximum character. April offering to bite Ron is perfectly April — the threat is primal, not metaphorical, and entirely sincere. Leslie's 'No' is great because it suggests she's considered it. The offer as protective loyalty is both sweet and absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron isn't even a real name. It's a sound you make when you're gargling.

jokes.text: Swanson, you didn't say anything about ambushing Leslie's press conference. / I didn't think it was relevant.
jokes.setup: Tom objects to Ron's ambush strategy.
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses the moral concern with 'I didn't think it was relevant' — treating Tom's objection as a logistical rather than ethical complaint.
jokes.explanation: Very Ron. 'I didn't think it was relevant' applied to an ethical concern about ambushing a former colleague is a perfect Ron deflection. He's not wrong that it's irrelevant — to him.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, your obsession with organizing binders and color-coding everything is the most tedious waste of human potential I've ever witnessed.

jokes.text: A heretofore unknown hunting lodge was recently discovered smack dab in the middle of the Newport land.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents her historical evidence at the press conference.
jokes.punchline: The audience knows the 'hunting lodge' is a pile of rubble with a bag of old hamburgers — the gap between her confident framing and what we've seen is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The joke is contextual — it lands because we know what the 'hunting lodge' actually is. Leslie's confident presentation of a garbage pile as a landmark is classic Parks and Rec dramatic irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: This feud between me and Ron is worse than Biggie and Tupac.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It's actually worse than the Freeman-Woodley feud.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? I've never heard of that.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Exactly. It was that bad.

jokes.text: Did Harrison plan his presidential campaign while sitting around the hearth which used to be there. Did he write letters to Thomas Jefferson on his rolltop desk, which, you know, I don't know, might have existed.
jokes.setup: Leslie is spinning historical significance at the press conference.
jokes.punchline: Her evidence crumbles mid-speech — 'which used to be there,' 'I don't know, might have existed' — as she loses confidence in real time.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's on-the-fly hedging mid-speech — 'which, you know, I don't know, might have existed' — is great cringe-character comedy. She's improvising historical facts in real time at a public event.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, come on. We need to work together on this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, Ben. I have principles.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What if I promise to name our first three children after Supreme Court justices? Thurgood, Ruth, and... Antonin.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You had me at Thurgood.

jokes.text: Don't believe me? Let's ask him. In the form of his direct descendant, Zachary.
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces her star witness, Harrison's 'direct descendant.'
jokes.punchline: The reveal of Zach, whose previous characterization (camp BO, boner) completely undercuts the setup of 'direct descendant speaking for history.'
jokes.explanation: The callback structure works well here — we've been prepared for Zach to disappoint, and the formal introduction maximizes the gap between expectation and reality.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, you two need to work this out. I'm locking you in here until you do.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, what? You can't just—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I can and I am. You're both acting like children, so I'm treating you like children.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is highly inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Is it? Because I'm about to take away your phones and make you share a juice box.

jokes.text: Uh... Harrison's a pretty common last name.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Zach what it's like to be a descendant of William Henry Harrison.
jokes.punchline: Zach's entire response is to note that Harrison is a common surname — entirely deflating the historical pageant.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan deflation. Zach's entire answer to 'what is it like to be descended from a president' is to question whether that's even meaningful given the surname frequency. Maximum economy, great structure. The contrast with Leslie's grandiose intro is the joke.

jokes.text: 'Wow, that was cool', said some boring idiot from 200 years ago.
jokes.setup: Leslie's team has just performed the Tippecanoe song with the tin ball.
jokes.punchline: Roscoe's dismissal of the entire presentation by attributing enthusiasm for it to a hypothetical 'boring idiot from 200 years ago.'
jokes.explanation: Great tech-bro dismissal of history. The specificity of 'boring idiot from 200 years ago' as the only demographic who would find the Tippecanoe ball exciting is well-worded. Roscoe's character register is perfectly maintained.

jokes.text: Here to introduce our vision is Annabel Porter from Bloosh, and the sexy ladies known in Pawnee as the Somebody's Daughter dancers.
jokes.setup: Gryzzl presents its competing vision at the press conference.
jokes.punchline: The troupe hired to make the presentation 'sexy' is locally known as 'the Somebody's Daughter dancers' — a name that implies parental concern and local infamy.
jokes.explanation: 'The Somebody's Daughter dancers' is an inspired name. It implies exactly what kind of troupe they are while giving them a name that radiates small-town scandal and parental disappointment. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Fresh. Innovative. Placemaking. Disposable duvets. Growth hacking. Super Moon. Gryzzl. Now, come with me, as we binge-watch the future.
jokes.setup: Annabel delivers Gryzzl's presentation as a series of lifestyle buzzwords.
jokes.punchline: 'Disposable duvets' appears amid legitimate-sounding tech/lifestyle jargon, and the whole thing culminates in 'binge-watch the future' — a meaningless tech-speak phrase delivered as a genuine slogan.
jokes.explanation: Good buzzword satire with 'disposable duvets' as the standout absurd entry in an otherwise plausible list of corporate jargon. 'Binge-watch the future' is the right closing beat — meaningless but confident.

jokes.text: It was exactly as substantive as your presentation.
jokes.setup: Leslie calls Gryzzl's presentation 'all flash, no substance.'
jokes.punchline: Ben points out that hers had identical substance — zero.
jokes.explanation: Ben's honest assessment of both presentations is a clean, economic line. Works as a gentle burn on Leslie and a fair observation.

jokes.text: No, it was not! We had way more quantity than you.
jokes.setup: Ron has said both presentations were equally thin.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense is 'We had way more quantity' — openly admitting quantity was the goal and that this constitutes a win.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff on 'Operation Quantity.' Leslie's straight-faced defense of quantity-over-quality as a criterion for victory is funny precisely because she says it without embarrassment.

jokes.text: Not that it matters. I'm definitely going to wake up tomorrow morning with the same forms for you to sign. Because I've died somehow and now I'm a ghost living in purgatory until I complete my unfinished business.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron are arguing again; the notary is frustrated.
jokes.punchline: Full articulation of the ghost-in-purgatory theory — his 'unfinished business' is a notarized document.
jokes.explanation: The third iteration of the ghost joke. Still working, but diminishing returns on originality. The structure is consistent but less impactful than earlier installments.

jokes.text: You can't stand my stupid mustache and my stupid shirt and my stupid name. Ron. Ron. That's not even a word.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a full argument with Ron.
jokes.punchline: Her insults escalate from mustache to shirt to name — and then she claims 'Ron' is not even a word, an objectively untrue statement delivered with full conviction.
jokes.explanation: 'Ron. Ron. That's not even a word.' is a great escalation. She's run out of substantive insults and has resorted to disputing the existence of a perfectly common English name. The repetition of 'Ron' as if trying to hear why it shouldn't be a word is a great beat.

jokes.text: You're not that good at scrapbooking.
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie are in a full-blown argument about their broken friendship.
jokes.punchline: Ron's final, unprovoked insult is about Leslie's scrapbooking ability — a completely unexpected pivot from the emotional high stakes.
jokes.explanation: The episode's second-best joke. After an increasingly emotional argument about betrayal and stubbornness, Ron's final blow is that Leslie is not that good at scrapbooking. The complete deflation of the drama, the randomness of the target, and the fact that Ron — a man who has never scrapbooked — is criticizing this hobby, is perfectly absurd. Maximum economy (six words), extremely quotable. Could only be Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Okay. Would you just sign right here? And I will need your thumbprints.
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie's argument has just reached peak absurdity.
jokes.punchline: The notary presses on, undeterred, now escalating to requiring thumbprints — as if the process keeps getting more elaborate.
jokes.explanation: Part of the notary running gag. The thumbprints addition is a mild escalation but the joke has been running long and this is among its weaker beats.

jokes.text: Man, those two really hate each other. That feud is, like, Biggie-Tupac level. Maybe even Morgan Freeman-Shailene Woodley level.
jokes.setup: Tom observes the Leslie-Ron feud.
jokes.punchline: He escalates the feud comparison from Biggie-Tupac (an actual legendary feud) to 'Morgan Freeman-Shailene Woodley' — implying a legendary feud between two people who have no known feud.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection. Starting with the legitimate Biggie-Tupac comparison and escalating to 'Morgan Freeman-Shailene Woodley' — two actors with no known animosity — as an even more legendary level of feud is a great absurdist escalation. Tom's confident delivery of this non-existent feud as common knowledge is very Tom.

jokes.text: Naw. It's bad, but it's not that bad.
jokes.setup: Tom suggests the Leslie-Ron feud might be 'Morgan Freeman-Shailene Woodley level.'
jokes.punchline: Andy's deadpan correction — accepting the Morgan Freeman-Shailene Woodley feud as real but placing the Leslie-Ron dispute below it in severity.
jokes.explanation: This is the perfect button to Tom's joke. Andy treating the Morgan Freeman-Shailene Woodley feud as real and measured — and determining Leslie-Ron doesn't quite reach that level — takes an already absurd premise and escalates it with straight-man conviction. The callback structure is excellent.

jokes.text: Actually, that might work. Have we tried that?
jokes.setup: Ben has said he can't give Leslie and Ron stuffed animals.
jokes.punchline: He immediately reconsiders — maybe he should try stuffed animals.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I can't do what I do with my toddlers' to 'wait, actually...' is a perfect comedic beat. Ben talking himself into trying the stuffed animal strategy on two middle-aged adults suggests both his desperation and his fundamental decency.

jokes.text: This is like when the triplets fight except I can't just give Leslie and Ron stuffed animals to make them calm down. Actually, that might work. Have we tried that?
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to mediate the Leslie-Ron situation.
jokes.punchline: He starts by comparing them to his young triplets, then realizes the triplet solution (stuffed animals) might actually work on two middle-aged adults — and is genuinely considering trying it.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I can't give them stuffed animals' to 'actually, that might work' is a great Ben joke — his earnest problem-solving applied to an absurd situation. The self-correction lands well.

jokes.text: Well, I ordered 60 veggie pizzas to Ron's office. So, that calmed me down a little.
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Leslie is okay after the confrontation with Ron.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals she ordered 60 pizzas to Ron's office as emotional self-regulation — and it worked.
jokes.explanation: The specific number (60), the specific variety (veggie — chosen to maximize Ron's horror), and the fact that it genuinely calmed her down are all well-chosen details. The petty act of vengeance as genuine self-soothing is very Leslie.

jokes.text: I'll let you rename the triplets Ruth, Bader, and Ginsburg.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to convince Leslie to sign the document with Ron.
jokes.punchline: His offer — letting Leslie name their triplets after Ruth Bader Ginsburg — reveals how well he knows his wife; this is the one incentive she cannot refuse.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Ben naming the triplets Ruth, Bader, and Ginsburg as the bribe is perfect character comedy — it works because it's exactly right about Leslie and because the triplets as a unit taking that name as a set is inherently funny. The joke is earned by seasons of Leslie's character. Extremely quotable, high rewatch value.

jokes.text: Okay, fine. But I get to sign first.
jokes.setup: Ben offers the triplet-naming deal; Leslie agrees.
jokes.punchline: Her condition — signing first — is a last tiny power play, revealing she cannot fully surrender the competition even when agreeing.
jokes.explanation: Good character button on the RBG triplet joke. Leslie's 'I get to sign first' is a miniature expression of her competitive nature — the negotiation continues to the very end.

jokes.text: Got them! / What? / What's going on? / Let us out immediately. / No. You guys are being ridiculous. This has gone too far, and you are not leaving this office until you've made peace.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron arrive to sign documents; Ben has set a trap.
jokes.punchline: Ben has locked both Leslie and Ron in the office — a physical comedy escalation where the mediator becomes the warden.
jokes.explanation: Ben's plan reveals a fun character dimension — the most exasperated person finally takes action. 'Let us out immediately' from both characters (presumably in unison) is a good moment. Works primarily as a physical escalation and episode button.

jokes.text: [Ben locks Leslie and Ron in his office together] No. You guys are being ridiculous. This has gone too far, and you are not leaving this office until you've made peace.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron come to sign the document in the same room.
jokes.punchline: Ben locks them both in — refusing to let them leave until they reconcile, treating them like feuding children.
jokes.explanation: Ben following through on the 'treat them like toddlers' impulse by literally locking them in a room is a satisfying structural payoff. His 'you are not leaving this office until you've made peace' lands because it completes the episode's main throughline.

tmdb_overview: Leslie's team tries to strengthen her case that the Newport land should be turned into a National Park. Ron's team, fighting back, brings on a celebrity as a minority owner.
insight: Season 7's densest episode delivers 69 jokes through pure character escalation.
